stimulus.attribution: Paraphrased from the argument of Eric Foner, Reconstruction: America's Unfinished Revolution, 1863-1877 (1988).
stimulus.text: During Reconstruction, formerly enslaved Black men voted in large numbers and held office at every level of Southern government, from local sheriffs and state legislators to members of Congress - a transformation made possible by the Reconstruction Acts and the Fifteenth Amendment. Historian Eric Foner has called Reconstruction 'America's unfinished revolution,' arguing that it was the first great experiment in interracial democracy, even though its gains were later overturned.

parts: A. Briefly explain Foner's view of the significance of Reconstruction for Black Americans.
B. Briefly explain one specific federal action between 1865 and 1877 that supports the developments Foner describes.
C. Briefly explain one development after 1877 that challenged the gains Foner describes.
exemplar: Foner views Reconstruction as America's 'unfinished revolution' - the first experiment in interracial democracy, in which Black men voted and held office across the South.
The Fifteenth Amendment (1870) prohibited denying the vote on account of race, giving constitutional protection to Black suffrage.

Southern states imposed poll taxes, literacy tests, and grandfather clauses that disenfranchised Black voters, while the Supreme Court weakened federal protection in decisions such as the Civil Rights Cases (1883).
questions.inspired_by: Chapter 5 Short-Answer Drill Q1 topic (Reconstruction voting)

stimulus.attribution: Source 1: Mary Rowlandson, taken captive during King Philip's War, 1675. Source 2: Henry Knox to George Washington, 1790s.
stimulus.text:
Source 1: 'It is a solemn sight to see so many Christians lying in their blood, some here, and some there, like a company of sheep torn by wolves, all of them stripped naked by a company of hell-hounds, roaring, singing, ranting, and insulting, as if they would have torn our very hearts out; yet the Lord by His almighty power preserved a number of us from death, for there were twenty-four of us taken alive and carried captive.'

Source 2: 'How different would be the sensation of a philosophic mind to reflect that instead of exterminating a part of the human race by our modes of population that we had persevered through all difficulties and at last had imparted our Knowledge of cultivating and the arts, to the Aboriginals of the Country by which the source of future life and happiness had been preserved and extended.'

parts: A. Briefly explain one major difference between Rowlandson's and Knox's views of Native Americans.
B. Briefly explain how the historical situation of ONE of the documents shaped the author's view.
C. Briefly explain one longer-term effect of the attitudes expressed in these documents on United States policy toward Native Americans.
exemplar: Rowlandson portrays Native Americans as savage 'hell-hounds' who slaughtered Christians, while Knox treats them as fellow members of the human race who could be 'civilized' through American knowledge of farming and the arts.
Rowlandson wrote as a captive during King Philip's War (1675-1676), when Wampanoag attacks had killed colonists and taken her prisoner; her terror shaped her demonizing language.

The view of Native peoples as either savage obstacles or candidates for 'civilization' underpinned removal and assimilation policies, from the Indian Removal Act of 1830 to the reservation and boarding-school systems.

The map reveals how rapidly European geographic knowledge expanded after 1492: within a decade, Portuguese cartographers could draw the coasts of Brazil and Africa in detail and mark a formal line dividing the world's oceans between Spain and Portugal.

The voyages were driven by the search for wealth - especially a sea route to the spices and riches of Asia and control of the African gold trade - which made kings willing to fund expensive, risky expeditions.

For Native peoples the voyages were catastrophic: European diseases such as smallpox, to which they had no immunity, killed enormous numbers, while conquest and the encomienda system destroyed communities across the Caribbean and the Americas.
parts: A. Briefly describe ONE thing the map reveals about European knowledge of the world after 1492.
B. Briefly explain ONE motive that drove the voyages of exploration recorded on the map.
C. Briefly explain ONE consequence of those voyages for Native peoples of the Americas.

stimulus.attribution: Described from the Cantino planisphere, anonymous Portuguese manuscript map, 1502.
stimulus.text: This large, richly decorated world map shows the coastlines of South America, Africa, and India drawn with remarkable new detail. A bold blue line - the line of demarcation - slashes across the Atlantic, dividing lands claimed by Spain from those claimed by Portugal. The Americas appear as newly found coasts, while Asia is still drawn from older, vaguer knowledge.
